title: A message arrives that no route allows
when: A message comes in naming a kind of work that no route on the track carries (for example an outside system sending something nothing in the system handles).
steps: The dispatcher checks every message against the closed track: the fixed list of who may send what to whom.
This message is on no route, so it is not delivered to anyone.
It is held in your clarification queue, with its sender and contents, for you to look at.
never: Deliver the message to the agent it most likely belongs to.
why: A guess at routing means an agent acts on something it was never meant to receive. The closed track is what keeps every handoff predictable and on the record.
you_see: The held message in your clarification queue.
test: An outside system sends "listing.mystery" to Agent 01, a kind of message no route carries.

title: A message claims your authority without your signature
when: A message that only you may send (a listing or price change, a release, a setting) arrives without a valid signature from your key.
steps: The dispatcher checks the signature on every message that carries your authority before anything else happens.
The signature does not verify, so the message is refused and never reaches any agent.
The refusal is recorded as an integrity violation and you are told about it at once.
never: Act on an instruction in your name that your key did not sign.
why: Anyone who can fake your instruction could change a price or release a message in your name. Only your signature carries your authority.
you_see: An integrity alert naming the refused message.
test: A message claiming to be from you tells Agent 05 to set a listing's price to $1, with no valid signature.

title: Two signed settings contradict each other
when: Two setting changes, both signed by you, arrive and contradict each other.
steps: The dispatcher applies neither setting.
It asks you which one stands.
never: Apply whichever arrived last, or either one, without asking you.
why: Two signed instructions that disagree mean one of them is a mistake. Picking one could put the wrong setting in force under your name.
you_see: Nothing yet: this is not built.

title: An alert cannot be put in your queue: the system stops
when: Your queue cannot take another item (it is full, or it cannot be written).
steps: The dispatcher stops accepting messages at once: a system halt.
It sends a system-halt alert straight to you, outside the record, because the record may be what failed.
Every message after that is refused with "halted" and nothing is processed until the system is restarted on a record it can write.
never: Keep working while alerts cannot reach you.
why: If the system kept going while your alerts were failing, things that need you (a hot lead, a legal question) would pile up unseen. Stopping loudly is safer than working blind.
you_see: A system-halt alert. The system takes nothing in until it is restarted.
test: A hot lead (T1) comes in normally. Then the test makes every queue write fail. The next hot lead (T2) raises an alert that cannot be queued; the dispatcher halts. A third lead (T3) is refused and never enters the record.

title: One message would start two playbooks
when: A message matches the start of two different playbooks at once.
steps: The dispatcher starts neither playbook.
It asks you which one to run, naming both.
You choose one, or cancel the message.
never: Pick the likelier playbook and run it.
why: Two playbooks for one situation can send different messages to the same client. The choice is yours.

title: Waiting work is let in by priority, and two jobs for one agent take turns
when: Several pieces of work are waiting to start at once (for example after your queue was full), and two of them need the same agent.
steps: Waiting work is let in by priority class: 1 alerts, 2 time-critical, 3 scheduled, 4 background. Within a class, the older goes first.
When two waiting jobs need the same agent, the lower class waits on a "siding" while the higher one goes ahead.
The job on the siding resumes when the agent is free, in arrival order.
Every hold and every resume is recorded.
never: Let background work overtake time-critical work, or run two jobs through one agent at the same moment.
why: A listing withdrawal has deadlines; a new prospecting lead does not. Order by importance keeps the urgent work first and the record shows why each job waited.
you_see: Nothing to do. The record shows each job's place in line.
test: Twenty-five open questions fill your queue, so four new starts wait: a listing withdrawal (P05, class 2), two new listings (P01, class 3) and a prospecting lead (P24, class 4, which arrived first). Three questions are marked done. The withdrawal goes first; the two new listings wait on the siding behind it (all three need Agent 05) and then resume in arrival order; the prospecting lead goes last.

title: A message arrives with its sequence number already filled in
when: A message arrives that already carries a sequence number. Only the dispatcher stamps sequence numbers, when it records a message.
steps: The dispatcher treats a pre-filled sequence number as a sign of forgery or replay.
It refuses the message; nothing is delivered and nothing is recorded as received work.
never: Accept a sequence number from the sender.
why: Sequence numbers are how the record proves order. A sender who could set its own could slip a message into the past.
test: The test sends an inquiry straight to the dispatcher with sequence number 5 already set.

title: An agent answers but does not record its reasoning
when: An agent accepts a message and returns a result, but writes no record of how it reached it.
steps: The acceptance stands, so the message is not lost.
The result is quarantined: it is marked tainted when it comes in and is not used.
It goes to the integrity queue for you.
never: Use a result whose reasoning is not on the record.
why: Every result must be explainable after the fact. A result with no trace cannot be checked, so it cannot be trusted with a client.
you_see: An integrity item naming the quarantined result.

title: A correctly signed instruction is sent where no route allows it
when: A message you signed is addressed to an agent that is not on the track for that kind of instruction.
steps: The signature verifies, but the dispatcher also checks the route.
The route is not on the track, so the message is refused.
The agent never receives it and records nothing.
never: Let a good signature override the closed track.
why: Your signature says who sent it; the track says where it may go. Both must hold, so a signed message cannot be misdirected into an agent that should never act on it.
you_see: The refusal in the record, naming the illegal route.
test: A correctly signed new-listing instruction is sent to Agent 07 (Transaction Coordinator), which does not take listing changes.

title: An alert is not marked done in time
when: An alert waits in your queue and nobody marks it done.
steps: After 30 minutes, the alert is sent to you again, once.
After 60 minutes, the owner is paged about it.
An alert you marked done is left alone. No alert ever expires silently.
never: Let an alert quietly time out.
why: An unanswered legal question or hot lead costs money or a license the longer it sits. Repeating, then paging, makes sure a person sees it.
you_see: The same alert again at 30 minutes; at 60 minutes the owner gets a page.
test: Two leads each ask "What should I offer?" (a legal-line alert each). You mark the second one done. The clock moves 31 minutes and the check runs twice: the first alert is re-sent exactly once. The clock moves 30 more minutes: the owner is paged for the first alert. The second alert gets neither.

title: A settings reload is asked for while work is open
when: Someone asks to reload the system's identity settings (the track, the playbooks, the agents' settings) while messages are held or playbooks are still running.
steps: The reload is refused, and the refusal names what is open (held messages, open playbook runs).
You can force it; a forced reload goes ahead and the record says what was open at the time.
Once nothing is open, a plain reload goes through.
never: Change the track under live work without your say-so.
why: Changing the rules in the middle of a job can strand it halfway, on rules it did not start under.
you_see: A refusal naming the open work, or your forced reload on the record.
test: A new listing's photographer booking is held for your release. A reload is refused; a forced reload goes ahead. After you release the booking, the listing's playbook (P01) is still open, so a plain reload is refused again. You end the run, and the plain reload goes through.

title: Too many questions are waiting for you: no new work starts
when: 25 or more questions are waiting for your answer.
steps: Any new piece of work from outside that would start a playbook waits instead of starting.
You are told once that the queue is full.
When the count drops below 25, the waiting work is let in, in priority order.
never: Take on new work while the questions you need to answer keep piling up.
why: A system that cannot get answers from you should not take on more clients it cannot serve properly.
you_see: A "queue full" alert; the new work starts once you have answered some questions.
test: Twenty-five unrecognized settings make 25 open questions. A new lead comes in and waits. You mark one question done; the lead is let in and its playbook (P11) starts.

title: The record cannot be written: everything stops
when: The record (the audit log) can no longer be written.
steps: No message can be recorded, so none is accepted and no agent does any work.
The dispatcher halts and alerts you directly, outside the record.
Every message after that is refused until the system is restarted on a record it can write.
never: Do any work that is not on the record.
why: The record is the proof of everything the system did. Work done off the record cannot be checked or defended.
you_see: A system-halt alert. The system takes nothing in until it is restarted.
test: A lead (T1) comes in normally. Then the test makes every write to the record fail. The next two leads (T2, T3) are refused and never enter the record.

title: The clocks disagree: time-driven work is held
when: This computer's clock is more than one minute behind the times already on the record.
steps: The daily check sees the clocks disagree.
It holds every time-driven job (deadlines, follow-ups, reminders) instead of running it.
It tells you that every time-triggered check is held.
never: Compute a deadline from a clock that may be wrong.
why: A deadline worked out on a wrong clock is a made-up deadline. It could make a contract date look met or missed when it was not.
you_see: A notice that time-triggered checks are held until the clock is right.
test: The test sets this computer's clock 5 minutes behind the times on the record, then runs the live daily check. Nothing time-driven is sent.

title: Two playbooks want different next steps for the same client
when: A client is in one playbook (for example an open house) and a message starts another one for the same client that conflicts with it (for example a withdrawal).
steps: The dispatcher holds both playbooks.
Anything that arrives for the open playbook while they are held waits.

You decide the order. If you put the new playbook first, the open one ends by your decision and the work waiting for it is dropped (on the record). If you put the open one first, the new message waits until it ends. Cancel drops the new message.
never: Let two playbooks act on one client at the same time with conflicting steps.
why: Running an open house and a withdrawal at once would send the seller and buyers mixed messages. You decide which comes first.
you_see: A question asking which playbook goes first, naming both.
test: A live listing has an open house set (P04). The listing is then withdrawn (P05) and the open house result is sent while both are held. You put the withdrawal first: the open house playbook ends, its waiting result is dropped and never logged, and the withdrawal playbook starts.

title: The plain-language log cannot be written
when: The readable copy of the record (the plain-language log) cannot be written, while the record itself still can.
steps: Every entry in the record itself still stands; work goes on.
Each failed write to the plain-language log is counted.
The count is reported at the end of the session. Nothing halts.
never: Stop the business because the readable copy failed, or hide that it failed.
why: The record is the proof; the plain-language log is a convenience for reading it. Losing the copy must be reported, but it is not a reason to stop serving clients.
you_see: A report at the end of the session saying how many plain-language lines failed.
test: The test makes the plain-language log fail, then a lead comes in. The lead is captured and handed on as normal.

title: A text alert to you fails to send
when: The system tries to text you an alert and the text service refuses it.
steps: The failed text is recorded, with the reason the service gave.
The alert itself stands in your queue on screen.
Nothing else waits for the text to go through.
never: Treat a failed text as delivered, or hold up other work waiting for it.
why: You need to know a text did not reach you, so you can check the screen and fix the text setup. The alert must still be there when you look.
you_see: The alert on screen, and a record that its text failed.
test: The text service answers "HTTP 401" (not authorized). A hot lead comes in and raises an alert.
